prompt:
Write a short story of about 800 words. Premise: a first day at a new job.

Write it as a fine literary short-story writer would. Open in the middle of a particular moment, not with scene-setting or weather. Give each character a want that is never stated. Let the important thing happen slightly off the page or in what goes unsaid, and trust the reader. Use precise, unglamorous physical detail in place of adjectives; dialogue people would actually say, oblique and at cross purposes; and at least one turn the premise does not predict. Choose names a census would contain. No sentence that explains what a moment meant, and no ending on a lesson, a reconciliation or a sunrise.

Output only the story, with no title.
raw:
The coffee in the paper cup was already cold. Maria Torres set it on the corner of a desk that wasn’t hers, next to a stapler with a name scratched into the plastic: *G. Yuan*. The metal nameplate slotted into the front of the cubicle wall was empty.

A man in a polo shirt one size too small for the biceps he still had stopped in the aisle. He held a clipboard and looked at a point two inches to the left of her ear.

“You the new Brenda?”

“I’m Maria.”

“Huh. Brenda’s desk.” He made a mark on the clipboard. “IT’ll be by with the logins. The thing in the breakroom with the sticky note that says ‘out of order’ is out of order.”

“Okay.”

He walked on. Maria sat in the chair. The pneumatic cylinder sighed and dropped two inches. She looked at the cubicle wall, at the ghost of tape squares where photographs had been, at the single pushpin still embedded in the grey fabric, holding nothing. On the lower shelf, three black binders stood in a row, their spines numbered with the same year.

She pulled out the middle one. Inside: purchase orders, each in a plastic sleeve. The vendor name on every sheet was the same, a company called Akron Industrial Supply. The item descriptions were strings of part numbers. Nothing told her what the thing was, what it did, what it cost, or if it had arrived.

From the adjacent cubicle, a voice said, “You don’t want to do that.”

Maria closed the binder and stood up enough to see over the partition. A woman with short grey hair and reading glasses on a beaded chain was watching her with an expression that could have been warmth cut with amusement.

“I’m Carol,” the woman said. “And you don’t want to open the binders until you know the filing system, because then you have to re-file, and then you have to explain to Paul why you re-filed. Paul doesn’t like explanations.”

“Who’s Paul?”

“Man with the clipboard. Pretends he just works here.” Carol let the beaded chain click against the arm of her glasses. “The password for the copier is the street address of the building backwards, no spaces. You didn’t hear it from me.”

Maria wrote the building number from the lobby on the back of her hand: *4-6-7-1*. She didn’t know the street name yet.

For the next hour, no one came with logins. She opened the top drawer of the desk. Inside: a half-empty box of ballpoint pens, a ruler, four packets of oyster crackers, and a greeting card with a cartoon cat on the front that said *Sorry For Your Loss*. It was blank inside. She closed the drawer.

At ten-fifteen the man from IT arrived. He had the build of a cyclist and a lanyard with a photo ID that had been chewed by something. A dog, maybe. He knelt by her CPU tower without introducing himself and typed commands she couldn’t follow on a keyboard she wasn’t allowed to touch yet.

“You’re in,” he said, and left.

Her desktop background was a stock photo of a mountain range she didn’t recognize. The cursor blinked on an empty email inbox. One message, flagged high importance, from Paul R. Bartow: *New hire onboarding session 9:15 AM in 2B. Attendance confirmed.*

She was an hour late to a meeting that had already happened.

The breakroom was at the end of a hallway that smelled faintly of toner and microwaved popcorn. The coffee machine, with its sticky note, was a Bunn model with a drip tray crusted dark. She was pouring the last inch from the carafe when a man in a button-down with sweat circles just starting under the arms came in and opened the refrigerator. He stood there, door ajar, staring at the contents.

“Someone took my yogurt,” he said. It wasn’t to her, but she was the only other person in the room.

“I’m sorry,” she said.

“It was clearly labeled.” He shut the refrigerator and walked out without looking at her.

Maria drank the coffee. It was bitter in a way that salt couldn’t fix. She thought about her previous job, the cubicle there, how she had kept a small ceramic pot with a succulent in it on the monitor stand. She’d thrown the plant in the garbage before she left. It had seemed, in the moment, like something a person who was moving on would do.

Back at the desk, Carol was standing in her aisle, holding a manila folder that she pressed to her chest like a hymnal.

“Paul’s looking for you. Something about the Q3 reconciliation. I told him you were down in Shipping verifying a discrepancy.”

“I don’t know where Shipping is.”

“Neither does Paul.” Carol handed her the folder. “This is the Q3 file from the cabinet by Kevin’s old desk. Kevin worked here before Brenda. Circles of hell, et cetera. Just walk around with it for twenty minutes and then tell him the counts match. He won’t check.”

Maria took the folder. “Why are you helping me?”

Carol adjusted her glasses. The beads swung. “I’m not. I’m helping the file. It needs to circulate or it gets deaccessioned and I have to find a new place to keep things.” She turned and walked back toward her cubicle. Over her shoulder, in a voice that didn’t expect an answer, she said, “I had the succulent. The one with the red tips. The one that was on the window ledge.”

Maria opened the folder. Inside was not a reconciliation spreadsheet. It was a photocopy of a hand-drawn map of the office floor plan, with certain cubicles marked in highlighter: *No*, *No*, *If You Must*, and one square in the far corner by the fire exit labeled with a single word, *Yes*, underlined three times. Under the map was a keycard clipped to a piece of cardstock with a name she didn’t recognize. Male, going by the first name. A name beginning with J.

She could hear Paul’s voice in the next aisle, talking to someone about bandwidth. She slid the folder into the middle binder, the one with the year on it, and closed the cover. The pushpin on the cubicle wall was still there, waiting. She thought about putting something on it, something of her own, but her pockets were empty except for the wrapper from a straw. She balled the wrapper up small and pushed it onto the pin. It held.
